    How to use this manual

    Read Part 1 once, then keep Flowdeck open next to this page and go through Parts 2–6 with the real screen in front of you. Part 7 turns everything into trades. Each lesson starts with a one-line summary. If a lesson feels heavy, read only the summary and the step-by-step box, and come back to the exact rules later. Screenshots come from Flowdeck's demo mode (a simulated market), so prices and sizes in them are made up.

    Part 1 · Foundations

    How the market actually works

    Two lessons with no Flowdeck buttons at all. Everything later builds on them.

    Lesson 1

    How price moves

    In one linePrice moves when impatient traders (market orders) use up the waiting orders (limit orders) at the current price, so the next trade has to happen at a worse price.

    Everything in Flowdeck shows one simple fight: people who want to buy against people who want to sell. Learn these words first and every screen will make sense.

    Think of a vegetable market. Shopkeepers put tomatoes on the shelf with a price tag and wait. Customers walk up and buy right now at the tag price. When customers buy all the cheap tomatoes, the next tomato on the shelf costs more. That is exactly how Bitcoin's price goes up.
    WordMeaningIn the market example
    Limit orderAn order that waits at a fixed price. It adds liquidity (stock on the shelf). The trader is called the maker.Shopkeeper's tomato with a price tag
    Market orderAn order that trades immediately with whatever is waiting. It removes liquidity. The trader is called the taker.Customer who buys right now
    Bid / AskBid = highest price a buyer is waiting at. Ask = lowest price a seller is waiting at.Best buy offer vs cheapest tag
    SpreadAsk minus bid. On Binance BTCUSDT it is usually $0.10, the smallest step.Gap between best offer and cheapest tag
    Order bookThe full list of waiting limit orders above and below the price.All shelves in the market
    AggressorThe side that used a market order. A trade counts as a buy if the buyer was the aggressor and a sell if the seller was.Who walked up to whom
    VolumeHow many BTC traded.Tomatoes sold today
    DeltaMarket buys minus market sells. +30 means aggressive buyers bought 30 BTC more than aggressive sellers sold.Customers buying vs customers dumping
    Perpetual (perp)A futures contract with no expiry that follows the Bitcoin price. Traders can use leverage and go short.A bet on the tomato price, settled every 8 hours
    SpotBuying real Bitcoin. No leverage, no funding.Taking the tomatoes home

    One trade, step by step

    1. A seller places a limit sell of 2 BTC at 85,001. Nothing trades yet; the order waits in the book as part of the ask.
    2. A buyer sends a market buy of 0.5 BTC. The exchange matches it with the cheapest waiting sell: 85,001.
    3. A trade prints: 0.5 BTC at 85,001. The buyer was the aggressor, so Flowdeck counts it as buy volume (green), and delta goes up by 0.5.
    4. The ask at 85,001 shrinks from 2 to 1.5 BTC. If buyers keep coming and take all 1.5, the next ask (say 85,002) becomes the best ask: price has moved up.
    Why this matters

    Every trade has a buyer and a seller, so "more buyers than sellers" is never literally true. What matters is who was in a hurry. The heatmap shows the patient side (limit orders). Bubbles, footprint and CVD show the hurried side (market orders). Order-flow trading is reading that fight.

    Practice tool

    Order book playground

    Buttons change the book
    Press Market buy 9 BTC. Watch the ask side get eaten and the price climb.

    Fees: maker vs taker

    Exchanges charge less for adding liquidity than for taking it. On Binance USDⓈ-M futures the base tier is about 0.02% maker and 0.05% taker (check your own tier; discounts exist). Fees are charged on the full position value, not on your margin.

    Worked example

    You buy 0.1 BTC at 85,000 with a market order and later sell with a market order at 85,100.

    Position value 0.1 × 85,000 = 8,500 USDT Entry fee (taker) 8,500 × 0.05% = 4.25 USDT Exit fee (taker) 8,510 × 0.05% = 4.26 USDT Gross profit 0.1 × 100 = 10.00 USDT Net profit 10.00 − 8.51 = 1.49 USDT

    A $100 move made only $1.49. Round-trip taker fees cost about $85 per BTC at this price. Small targets with market orders rarely pay.

    Leverage, margin and liquidation

    Leverage lets you hold a position bigger than your money. With 10× leverage, 1,000 USDT of margin controls a 10,000 USDT position. A 1% price move then changes your margin by 10%. When losses eat almost all the margin, the exchange closes the position for you with a market order: a liquidation. A long liquidation is a forced sell; a short liquidation is a forced buy.

    The approximate formula (the same one Flowdeck's liquidation model uses)
    • Long liquidates near entry × (1 − 1/leverage + 0.4%)
    • Short liquidates near entry × (1 + 1/leverage − 0.4%)
    • 0.4% is a typical maintenance margin. Real exchanges use tiers by position size and also count fees, so treat this as an estimate.
    LeverageLong from 85,000 liquidates nearDistanceShort from 85,000 liquidates near
    5×68,340−19.6%101,660
    10×76,840−9.6%93,160
    25×81,940−3.6%88,060
    50×83,640−1.6%86,360
    100×84,490−0.6%85,510

    A 100× long dies on a 0.6% dip, which BTC can do in a minute. That is why liquidations cluster just below recent buying and just above recent selling, and why Lesson 9 maps them.

    Funding and open interest

    Funding rate

    Every 8 hours (00:00, 08:00, 16:00 UTC = 05:30, 13:30, 21:30 IST) one side pays the other a small percentage of the position value. Positive funding: longs pay shorts, so most traders are long. The normal baseline on Binance is 0.0100% per 8 hours.

    10,000 USDT long × 0.0100% = 1 USDT per 8 h (3 per day) 10,000 USDT long × 0.0500% = 5 USDT per 8 h (15 per day)

    High positive funding = crowded longs who are paying to stay in. Crowds get squeezed.

    Open interest (OI)

    The number of perpetual contracts still open. Every contract has one long and one short, so OI tells you how many positions exist, not their direction.

    New long buys from new short → OI +1 Old long sells to new short → OI 0 (position handed over) Old long sells to old short → OI −1 (both close)

    OI rising = fresh positions (fuel). OI falling = people leaving (often profit taking or liquidations).

    Beginner mistakes
    • Thinking a big green trade guarantees an up move. Someone sold that BTC to the buyer; if the seller is bigger and patient, price can still fall.
    • Choosing leverage first. Risk comes from your stop distance and position size (Lesson 26); leverage is only what results.
    • Ignoring fees. With market orders in and out, every trade starts about 0.1% of position value in the red.
    • Reading OI as "bullish" or "bearish" on its own. OI only says positions opened or closed. Pair it with price and CVD (Lesson 12).
    Lesson 2

    The six kinds of players

    In one lineDifferent players leave different footprints. Flowdeck is a tool for spotting which of them is active right now.

    🏦

    Market makers

    What they do
    Keep bids and asks on both sides all day and earn the spread. They want small inventory, not direction.
    Where in Flowdeck
    Most of the colour on the heatmap; the flicker in the pull/stack strip.
    The tell
    When they get scared they pull quotes: the heatmap goes darker, the spread widens and pull/stack turns red. Big moves often follow.
    🐋

    Whales and funds

    What they do
    Move hundreds or thousands of BTC. They cannot buy all at once without pushing price against themselves, so they split orders, hide them (icebergs) or buy into other people's selling (absorption).
    Where in Flowdeck
    Numbered circles, the ≥ 10 BTC line in "CVD by order size", icebergs, absorption, spot CVD and the Coinbase premium.
    The tell
    Price stops falling while selling continues, or whale CVD rises while small-trader CVD falls.
    🎰

    Leverage traders

    What they do
    Use perps with leverage, chase breakouts and pay funding. Many are retail; some are fast prop traders.
    Where in Flowdeck
    Open interest, funding, perps CVD, liquidation markers.
    The tell
    OI rising fast, funding high and a "perp-led" move without spot buying = a crowd that can be squeezed.
    🧮

    Options dealers

    What they do
    Sell options on Deribit and hedge by buying or selling Bitcoin as price moves.
    Where in Flowdeck
    Gamma tab, call wall, put wall, gamma flip, max pain.
    The tell
    In positive gamma price gets "sticky" near big strikes. In negative gamma moves speed up.
    ⚙️

    The liquidation engine

    What it does
    Not a person: the exchange's robot that closes losing leveraged positions with market orders, whatever the price.
    Where in Flowdeck
    Orange and cyan diamonds, cascade boxes, the liquidation map, OI drops.
    The tell
    Forced orders overshoot. When a cascade ends, price often snaps back.
    🎭

    Spoofers

    What they do
    Place large orders they do not want filled, to scare or attract other traders, then cancel them.
    Where in Flowdeck
    Amber ✕ "pulled" markers; walls that move away as price comes close.
    The tell
    A level where walls keep getting pulled is not support or resistance, however red it looks.
    Who wins? At any price, price breaks when the market orders arriving there are bigger than the limit orders waiting there. Market orders are the attack, limit orders are the defence. Every Flowdeck panel shows one of the two sides.
    PanelShows the attack (market orders)Shows the defence (limit orders)
    HeatmapBubbles and numbered circlesColoured price rows, walls, depth ladder
    FootprintEvery number in the cellsIndirectly: big volume with no price progress = a big limit order
    Lower paneDelta, CVD, CVD by size–
    Book tabFillsWalls, pull/stack, icebergs
    MarkersLiquidations, cascadesPulled / filled walls, icebergs, absorption

    What every area of the screen is, what each number at the top means, and how to set the app up before you start.

    Lesson 3

    A tour of the whole screen

    In one lineTop bar = market vital signs, toolbar = what to show, big chart = order book and trades, lower pane = who is pushing, side panel = details.

    Tap any yellow number to learn what that part does. On a phone, press Zoom and swipe sideways.

    Your first five minutes

    1. Check the connection. Top right must say Live, not "Demo feed". Never trade from Demo.
    2. Check the accuracy badge. A green dot and "Trades N/N min exact" means Flowdeck matches Binance minute by minute. Give it 2–3 minutes after starting.
    3. Pick the book. Start with Binance. Switch to All books when you want to see if a wall lives on Bybit or OKX.
    4. Set sizes. Toolbar Min 0.2–0.5 BTC hides tiny trades. Use the green bubble size slider until bubbles are easy to see but do not cover the heatmap. Layers ▾ → Big trade 5 BTC on normal days, 10–20 BTC on busy days, so only real size gets a numbered circle.
    5. Turn on levels. Layers ▾: Gamma levels, Prior sessions + naked POCs (3 days), VWAP Daily with ±σ bands, volume profile Session. These are your map.
    6. Lower pane on "Delta + CVD", side panel on Tape. Now read Lesson 4.
    Beginner mistakes
    • Turning every layer on at once. Start with the defaults and add one layer at a time until you know what it looks like.
    • Zooming the heatmap out to hours. It only keeps 30 minutes; use Footprint or TPO for longer views.
    • Reloading the page in the middle of a session and wondering why CVD changed. CVD restarts from what your browser loaded (Lesson 11).

    Worked example: reading the top bar in the screenshot
    Price 83,979 · 24h −0.97% · Funding 0.0081% · OI 82,020 BTC OI all venues 147.1k, +943 in 1h · CB premium +$14.5 · Trades 39/39 exact
    • Price down about 1% in a day, funding a little below normal: sellers are pushing, but nobody is crowded.
    • OI +943 BTC in an hour while price fell: new positions opened on the way down, most likely new shorts (check the OI pane, Lesson 12).
    • US buyers still pay $14.5 more on Coinbase: real spot buyers are not selling.
    • Data is exact: safe to read. Conclusion: fresh shorts are pressing, but spot holds up. Shorting late into support is risky; if selling stalls at a level, those new shorts can get squeezed (Setup C or D, long versions).

    Part 3 · Heatmap & order book

    Seeing the waiting orders and the hits

    The heatmap is Flowdeck's main screen. These six lessons explain the picture, the trades on top of it, the walls, hidden orders, absorption and liquidations, with the exact rules Flowdeck uses to mark each one.

    Lesson 5

    Reading the heatmap

    In one lineLeft to right is time, bottom to top is price, and the colour of each price row is how many BTC are waiting there at that moment: blue few, grey more, yellow → orange → red a lot. Red stripes are walls; dark gaps are where price can move fast.

    Colour scale

    Nothing waitingNormal (blue)More (grey)Big (yellow)Wall (red)

    This is the Classic colour set (Layers ▾ → Heatmap → Colours), the one most order-flow tools use. Thermal (teal → yellow → white, no rows) is the older Flowdeck look.

    How Flowdeck builds the picture
    • Binance sends order-book changes every 100 ms. Every 250 ms Flowdeck records one column: the BTC waiting at every $1 price (bids below price, asks above).
    • Price rows: the $1 steps are added up into rows. Auto picks $1, 2, 5, 10, 20, 25 or 50 so each row is about 10 pixels tall at your zoom; Layers ▾ → Heatmap → Price rows can fix the size. A thin dark line separates the rows, and dotted vertical lines follow the time axis.
    • When you zoom out so far that one pixel holds several 250 ms columns, Flowdeck averages them, so steady orders show as steady stripes instead of flicker.
    • Each column covers ±$800 around the price. The last 30 minutes are kept. History starts when the server starts; nobody records order books for free, so it cannot be downloaded.
    • The colour scale is logarithmic and relative: it is anchored on the typical (median) row on your screen. A row about 4× the typical size or more reaches red; the contrast slider moves that point. So "red" means big compared with what is on screen, not a fixed number of BTC. Hover to see the real size.
    • Binance's snapshot only reaches 1,000 levels per side (about ±$100–150). Deeper levels fill in as they change, so far-away prices may look emptier at first.

    Read it step by step

    1. Find the price. It is where the bubbles are, between the green best-bid line and the red best-ask line.
    2. Look up and down for yellow, orange and red stripes within $100–300 of price. The nearest one above is the first resistance, the nearest below the first support.
    3. Check how long each line has been there. A line that runs across the whole screen is a patient order. One that appeared seconds ago, just ahead of price, is suspicious.
    4. Look for dark gaps. A dark band means few orders: if price enters it, it can travel fast to the next yellow or red area.
    5. Watch what happens when price touches a red stripe: it holds, gets pulled, gets eaten, or turns out to be an iceberg (Lesson 7).
    6. Hover any spot to see the exact BTC resting there on Binance and on the other books, the total of that price row, and the trades at that price.

    Patterns to recognise

    Long steady wall

    A red or orange stripe that stays for many minutes. Someone really wants that price. The longer it stays as price comes near, the more it matters.

    Wall that follows price

    A yellow or red stripe that keeps the same distance from price, moving up and down with it. Often a spoof or a market maker leaning. It usually disappears when price comes for it.

    Dark gap (liquidity void)

    A band with almost no orders. Price crosses voids quickly. Good for targets, bad for stops (your stop fills worse there).

    Round-number band

    Extra orders at 84,000, 84,500, 85,000. Many people put orders at round prices, so these often slow price down.

    Book thinning everywhere

    The whole screen turns darker blue. Market makers are pulling quotes, usually before news or after a shock. Expect bigger, faster moves.

    Walls stepping back

    As price approaches, the wall is cancelled and a new one appears further away. The defenders are retreating, so price tends to keep going in that direction.

    The two thin lines and the crosshair box

    The green line is the best bid, the red line the best ask (switch: Layers ▾ → Bid / ask). The gap between them is the spread; on BTC it is usually one $0.10 tick, so the lines touch. A gap that opens up means the book is thin right at the price. The crosshair box shows price and time under the mouse, "Resting X BTC @ $1" on Binance, "other books" with what Bybit and OKX have at that price (shown even when the heatmap is on Binance only), and the trades printed there.

    "All books" view

    What "All books" adds
    • Bybit's USDT perpetual book (1,000 levels) and OKX's BTC-USDT swap book are added to Binance's, at every $1 price.
    • Each exchange trades at a slightly different price (the basis, usually a few dollars). Flowdeck shifts each book by its basis so that the same "real" price lines up.
    • An exchange whose book is out of sync is left out until it recovers. Bybit's inverse contract is not included.

    A wall that shows up only with All books lives on another exchange. Big walls on all three exchanges at the same price are stronger than one.

    Beginner mistakes
    • Treating "red" as a fixed size. Zoom out and a 60 BTC wall can turn blue next to a 300 BTC one, and bigger price rows add more orders together. Hover for the number.
    • Expecting every wall to hold. Many walls are pulled before price arrives (Lesson 7). A wall is a clue, not a promise.
    • Putting your stop exactly at a wall. Everyone sees it; stops cluster just beyond it and get swept. Put stops a little past it.
    • Caring about walls 1–2% away. Only walls that price can reach in the next minutes matter now.
    Lesson 6

    Trade bubbles and big orders

    In one lineBubbles are trades that already happened: a green ball means more was bought at market, a red ball more was sold. A circle with a number is one single big market order.

    Trade bubbles: how they are drawn
    • Binance trades are used, plus other perpetual exchanges' trades (shifted by their basis) when "Other venues' prints" is on. Spot trades are not.
    • Grouping (Layers ▾ → Bubbles): Smart (default) puts all trades of a short time slot (about 48 pixels wide) and a price band into one bubble, placed at their average time and price. 1 s, 5 s, 15 s, 1 min use fixed time slots. Off draws every $1 price in every 250 ms column.
    • Style: 3D shaded balls (default), 2D dots, or a Buy/sell pie (green slice = market buys, red slice = market sells). In 3D and 2D the colour is the side that traded more.
    • Size by: Total volume (buys + sells) or Volume delta (buys − sells, so a big ball means one side clearly won). Size grows with the square root: 4× the BTC makes a ball 2× wider.
    • Size slider 0.4×–6× (also the green slider on the toolbar) and Transparency 0–90% (default 25%) so you can see the heatmap through the balls.
    • Bubbles smaller than the toolbar Min (default 0.2 BTC) are hidden. Big ones are drawn first, so small ones stay visible on top.
    Big orders: how Flowdeck rebuilds one market order
    • Exchanges report a big market order as many small fills. On Binance, fills with the same timestamp and side arriving within 120 ms are glued back into one sweep. The price is the average fill price.
    • If the sweep is at least Big trade (default 5 BTC; options 2–100), it is drawn as a circle with its size. For Binance orders, a white vertical line through it shows the price range it ate through, when that is $1 or more.
    • Other exchanges are rebuilt the same way, each with its own grouping key (Bybit's sequence number, OKX's timestamp, Coinbase's order id, Binance spot and COIN-M timestamps), within 150 ms, placed at their price minus their basis, and labelled: BIN-C COIN-M, BYB Bybit, BYB-I Bybit inverse, OKX, BIN-S Binance spot, CB Coinbase. Spot exchanges get a dashed circle.
    • The Tape tab lists every sweep of at least 0.5 BTC (filter "Show ≥", default 1 BTC). Rows at least the Big trade size are highlighted.
    Worked example: one tape row
    14:30:17.221 BIN 84,901.1 27.7 ×29 $2.3M

    At 14:30:17.221 one market buy (green) of 27.7 BTC hit Binance. It was filled in 29 pieces, at an average of 84,901.1, worth $2.3 million. On the heatmap it is a green circle labelled 27.7 with a white line from the lowest to the highest fill price. 29 fills means it ate through many price levels: someone was in a hurry.

    Read a big order in five questions

    1. Which side? Green = an impatient buyer, red = an impatient seller.
    2. How big compared with normal? 5 BTC is big on a quiet Sunday and small during the US open. Tune Big trade so you see a few circles per minute, not dozens.
    3. Where? A big order at a key level (yesterday's high, VAH, a wall) matters much more than one in the middle of nowhere.
    4. What happened next? Price moved in its direction = initiative (it worked). Price did not move or reversed = absorbed (someone bigger was on the other side) and the trader may be trapped.
    5. Are there more? Several big circles on the same side within seconds = urgency. One lonely circle = one trader.
    Beginner mistakes
    • "A big green circle means up." Big buyers get trapped at highs all the time. Judge by what price does next.
    • Ignoring the exchange label. A 20 BTC Coinbase spot buy (dashed) and a 20 BTC Binance perp buy mean different things: real coins vs a leveraged bet.
    • Setting Big trade to 1 BTC. The screen fills with circles and the important ones disappear in the noise.
    • Making bubbles so big they hide the walls. Lower the size slider or raise Transparency until you can see the price rows behind them.
    Lesson 7

    Walls, pull/stack and icebergs

    In one lineA wall is an unusually big waiting order. What matters is what happens to it when price arrives: held, pulled, eaten, or refilled from a hidden iceberg.

    What counts as a wall
    • Every 5 seconds Flowdeck looks at all Binance price levels within ±0.25% of the price and takes the median size (the typical level).
    • Wall threshold = the larger of 15 BTC and 10 × that median. Any single price level at or above it, within 1.5% of the price, is tracked as a wall.
    • The W 104 tags on the right edge of the heatmap are the 24 biggest walls right now (refreshed every second), with their current size.
    • In the heatmap's depth ladder, a row that contains a tracked wall gets an amber box (Binance book only; rows get wider as you zoom out). In the Book tab ladder, any $1 row at or above the threshold is highlighted.
    Worked example: the threshold
    Quiet book: median level 1.2 BTC → 10 × 1.2 = 12 → threshold = 15 BTC (the floor) Busy book: median level 2.4 BTC → 10 × 2.4 = 24 → threshold = 24 BTC
    How Flowdeck decides what happened to a wall
    • Every size decrease on Binance is held for 350 ms and matched with trades at that exact price (up to 700 ms later). The matched part was filled; the rest was cancelled.
    • A wall ends when it falls below 20% of its biggest size (if it comes back above 50%, it is still alive).
    • Pulled (amber ✕): at least 60% of what disappeared was cancelled, and price was within 8 bps (0.08%, about $68 at 85,000) at the end. Label "pulled N" when N is big.
    • Filled (small square, "wall filled N"): at least 50% of what disappeared actually traded.
    • A wall cancelled while price was far away gets no marker: that is just a trader moving an order.
    Worked example: a pulled wall
    Wall at 84,600, biggest size 65 BTC. Price falls to 84,640. It drops to 7 BTC: 52 cancelled + 6 traded = 58 gone. Cancelled share 52 ÷ 58 = 90% (≥ 60% ✓) Distance 40 ÷ 84,600 = 4.7 bps (≤ 8 bps ✓) Result amber ✕ "pulled 52"

    Anyone who bought at 84,610 "because of the wall" now has no support under them. That is exactly what a spoofer wants.

    Practice: four things can happen at a wall

    Practice tool

    Wall outcome simulator

    Pull / stack: are the orders arriving or leaving?

    Right of the heatmap's price axis sits the depth ladder: green bars are waiting buy orders, red bars waiting sell orders, as they are right now.

    The thin strip between the price axis and the ladder is pull/stack. For each price it shows orders added minus orders cancelled over the last 30 seconds (Layers ▾ → Pull / stack: off, 5, 30 or 60 s). Green to the right = more added (stacking). Red to the left = more cancelled (pulling). Orders that traded are not counted as pulls, thanks to the trade matching above.

    The Book tab shows the same numbers as a table, plus:

    • Walls now ≥ threshold: side, price, size, age and distance in bps.
    • Wall events & icebergs: a pulled wall reads "52 of 65 cancelled" (cancelled out of the wall's biggest size), a filled wall "40 of 61 filled", an iceberg "11.0 traded, 3.0 shown".
    • Totals since start: added, cancelled, filled, hidden.
    Reading it: bids stacking under price while asks are being pulled above it = buyers getting ready and sellers stepping away. That leans up. The opposite leans down.

    Icebergs: hidden orders

    Big traders often show only a small part of their order. Each time the visible part is filled, it refills. On the heatmap the level never looks big, yet a lot trades there and price does not get through.

    Iceberg rule
    • Flowdeck tracks every exact price where trades hit resting orders, for up to 60 seconds.
    • "Hidden" volume = traded volume that no visible size decrease explains within 1.5 seconds.
    • It marks a cyan ◇ "iceberg X (Y hidden)" when at least 4 BTC traded there, and (half or more was hidden or more than twice the largest size ever shown traded), and (the size refilled at least twice or 60% or more was hidden). At most one marker per price every 30 s.
    Worked example
    Ask at 84,710 never shows more than 3 BTC. In 40 seconds 11 BTC of market buys trade there; the size refilled 4 times. Traded 11 ≥ 4 ✓ · 11 > 2 × 3 ✓ · refills 4 ≥ 2 ✓ → "iceberg 11 (8 hidden)"

    A hidden seller sits at 84,710. Buyers will need much more than the visible 3 BTC to get through.

    Beginner mistakes
    • Trusting a wall that appeared seconds before price got there. Real defenders usually wait patiently.
    • Forgetting history. A price where walls were pulled three times today is a spoof zone, not support.
    • Thinking an iceberg is unbeatable. It has a size too. When it is finally eaten, the break is often fast.
    Lesson 8

    Absorption: the invisible defender

    In one lineLots of market orders hit one price, more than was ever visibly waiting there, and the price still did not break. Someone hidden took the other side.

    Illustration

    Absorption vs a normal break

    ▲ absorb

    Drawings, not screenshots. On the heatmap absorption is a violet dashed line with a ▲ and "absorb X"; on the footprint it is a violet box around the cell.

    Absorption rule (Binance trades, every $1 price, each side separately)
    • Enough selling (or buying): in the last 8 seconds, market orders at this price total at least the larger of 5 BTC and 25% of the average 10-second market volume (an average that updates every 10 s).
    • More than was visible: that volume is at least the largest size ever shown resting at this price since the tracking started.
    • Price held: the best bid (for selling) never went more than $1 below the level, or the best ask (for buying) more than $1 above it.
    • All three hold for 1.5 seconds → marker. Selling absorbed = "Bid held"; buying absorbed = "Offer held". The ratio = volume ÷ largest visible size.
    • Scored after 60 seconds: did price move away in the defended direction? The Signals tab shows how many were scored, the % that held direction and the average move.
    Worked example
    Average 10-second market volume: 120 BTC → threshold max(5, 0.25 × 120) = 30 BTC In 6 seconds, 38 BTC of market sells hit the bid at 84,650. Most ever shown at 84,650: 18 BTC → 38 ≥ 18 ✓ (ratio 2.1×) Best bid stayed at 84,649.9 or higher → held ✓ for 1.5 s Result: ▲ "absorb 38.0" at 84,651 (the middle of the $1 step), Signals row "Bid held · 38.0 BTC · 2.11×" 60 s later price is 84,712 → scored +62, held direction ✓

    How to use absorption

    1. Only at a level. Absorption at VAL, a put wall, yesterday's low or a big wall means something. In the middle of nowhere it is noise.
    2. Wait for the reaction. The defender proved itself only if price then moves away. A green bar closing back above the level is your trigger (Setup A).
    3. Check today's score. In the Signals tab, "Held direction" below about 55% means today's absorptions are not working well; lean on other clues.
    4. Absorption can fail. If price breaks the level after absorption, the defender was filled or gave up. Those breaks are often fast.

    In our live test, absorption held direction about half the time on its own. Its value comes from confluence: absorption plus a key level plus a footprint that agrees.

    The screenshot shows "No absorption yet": the demo market rarely produces it.

    Beginner mistakes
    • Buying every "Bid held" marker. Half of them fail. Use them as one vote, not the decision.
    • Missing absorption on the other side: "Offer held" at a high while everyone is buying is a short clue, not a long one.
    • Forgetting the stop. If the absorbed level breaks by more than a few dollars, the idea is wrong.
    Lesson 9

    Liquidations, cascades and the liquidation map

    In one lineLiquidations are forced market orders. When many fire together they push price further and trigger more of them (a cascade). The liquidation map estimates where the next pool of them sits.

    Liquidation markers
    • Sources: both Binance perpetuals, Bybit (USDT and inverse) and OKX. Each is placed at its price minus that exchange's basis.
    • ◆ orange = a long was liquidated (forced sell). ◆ cyan = a short was liquidated (forced buy). Size label when it is at least 2 BTC (or half the Big trade size, if bigger).
    • Important: Binance publishes at most one liquidation per second per contract, so its numbers are a sample. Bybit and OKX send all of them.
    Cascade rule
    • Every 10 seconds Flowdeck adds up the liquidations of the last 30 seconds on each side, across all exchanges.
    • If that total is at least the larger of 20 BTC and 4× the recent normal amount, it draws a shaded box "Long liq cascade 85 BTC" (orange) or "Short liq cascade" (cyan) and logs it in the Signals tab. Then that side waits 60 s before it can fire again.

    The liquidation map (a model)

    Exchanges do not publish where traders will be liquidated. Flowdeck estimates it from open interest: when OI rises, new positions were opened somewhere near the current price, and they will be liquidated at predictable distances.

    How the model works
    • Every 3 seconds Flowdeck reads Binance OI. If it rose, the new positions are placed at the average trade price (VWAP) of those 3 seconds, on both sides. The side that was aggressive gets full weight, the passive side half weight.
    • Leverage mix assumed: 5× 10%, 10× 25%, 25× 30%, 50× 22%, 100× 13%. Each part's liquidation price uses the formula from Lesson 1 (0.4% maintenance).
    • If OI falls, all levels shrink in proportion. Levels that price has already traded through are deleted (those traders are gone). Old levels fade with a 48-hour half-life.
    • The start-up uses the last ~42 hours of 5-minute OI history. Levels are grouped in $25 steps; the 4 biggest clusters each side get a dashed line "liq ~N".
    • Drawn as a histogram on the right edge of the heatmap: orange below price (longs), cyan above (shorts). The Flow tab lists the clusters.
    Practice tool

    Where would these traders be liquidated?

    Same formula as the model

    How to use liquidations

    1. Clusters are magnets. Big players need someone to trade against. A pool of stop and liquidation orders is guaranteed volume, so price is often pushed into big clusters.
    2. Clusters are fuel. When price reaches a long cluster, forced sells speed the drop up (cascade). Do not buy into a running cascade.
    3. After the cascade, look for the turn. When liquidations stop, OI has dropped and absorption or an iceberg appears at the low, the forced sellers are done (Setup D).
    4. Watch the OI pane. Orange ticks from the bottom = long liquidations; cyan from the top = short liquidations; a big OI drop confirms the flush.
    Beginner mistakes
    • Treating the map as real data. It is an estimate from Binance OI with an assumed leverage mix.
    • "Catching the knife": buying while orange diamonds are still streaming in.
    • Forgetting that Binance's liquidation feed is a sample. Small Binance totals do not mean small liquidations.

    Markers are clues, not orders

    No single marker is a reason to trade. They become useful when two or three agree at an important price (Lesson 24).

    Part 4 · Who is pushing

    Delta, CVD, open interest and leadership

    The heatmap shows where orders wait. These lessons show who is attacking, whether new money is arriving, and whether real spot buyers or leveraged traders lead the move.

    Lesson 11

    The lower pane: six ways to see pressure

    In one lineDelta is buyers minus sellers right now; CVD adds it up over time. If price and CVD disagree, the move is weaker than it looks.

    Delta = market buys minus market sells. CVD (cumulative volume delta) is the running total of delta. A rising CVD line means aggressive buyers have been winning. Pick a mode with the toolbar selector; each tab below shows a real screenshot, the exact definition, how to read it and an example.

    Divergence: the most useful CVD pattern

    Bearish divergence

    Price makes a higher high, CVD makes a lower high. Buyers pushed less hard to get the new high, or a seller absorbed them. Up-moves are getting weaker.

    Bullish divergence

    Price makes a lower low, CVD makes a higher low. Sellers are running out, or a buyer is absorbing them. Down-moves are getting weaker.

    Beginner mistakes
    • Comparing CVD values across a reload. CVD starts at whatever your browser loaded, so only its shape and direction matter.
    • Trading a divergence alone. It says "weaker", not "reverse now". Wait for a level and a trigger.
    • Comparing the size of the spot and perps lines. Each is scaled on its own; compare their direction.
    Lesson 12

    Price, open interest and CVD together

    In one linePrice says what happened, CVD says who attacked, OI says whether positions were opened or closed. Together they tell you the story behind a move.

    Where to read each in Flowdeck: price on the chart; CVD in "Delta + CVD" or "Perps CVD by venue"; OI in "OI Δ + liquidations", the top bar "OI all venues · 1h" or the footprint's OI Δ row. Look at the last 5–30 minutes.

    Practice tool

    Decoder: pick what you see

    12 combinations
    Price
    Open interest
    CVD
    Flowdeck's own OI labels (OI pane and footprint OI Δ row)
    • new longs OI up and price up (or flat)
    • new shorts OI up and price down
    • longs out OI down and price down (or flat)
    • shorts out OI down and price up. In the OI pane these read "Longs closing" and "Shorts covering".
    • These labels use only OI and price. Adding CVD (the decoder) tells you whether the openers or closers were aggressive.
    Lesson 13

    Flow tab: spot, perps and every exchange

    In one lineThe Flow tab answers "is this move real?": real spot buying, or leverage that can unwind?

    Leadership card: who moved price in the last 5 minutes, how far (bps), for how long, and the running score of past calls.

    Coinbase premium in $ and bps · USDT/USD from Coinbase · OI all venues with 5-minute and 1-hour change · Funding (OI-weighted): each exchange's funding weighted by its OI · Liquidations 1h long / short in BTC.

    Venues table: for each exchange a live dot (message in the last 30 s), price, basis to Binance, OI and funding. The tick box hides that exchange from the tape, the per-venue CVD lines and the markers. It does not change the totals in this tab, which always use every exchange.

    Spot vs perps delta (5 min and 1 hour): perps = all perpetuals including Binance; spot = Binance spot + Coinbase.

    Delta by order size (perps): rebuilt market orders split into < 1 BTC, 1–10 BTC and ≥ 10 BTC. "≥ 10 BTC" is whale money.

    Liquidation levels (model): the biggest estimated clusters, shorts above and longs below (Lesson 9).

    How the leadership call is made
    • Every 10 seconds Flowdeck looks at the last 5 minutes (it needs at least 2). It measures the price change in bps and, separately for perps and for spot, the aggression: (buy − sell) ÷ (buy + sell) of market orders.
    • Aggression above 0.08 counts as "buying", below 0.02 as "not buying" (mirror for selling).
    • Price change ≥ +12 bps (≈ $100 at 85,000) or ≤ −12 bps decides the up/down labels; within ±6 bps the divergence labels can fire.
    • Each call is checked 5 minutes later against the direction Flowdeck expects. The hit rate over the last 400 calls is shown.
    LabelConditionFlowdeck expectsWhy
    Spot-led rallyUp ≥ 12 bps, spot buying, perps notContinuation upReal buyers own the coins and rarely panic.
    Broad buying (spot + perps)Up, both buyingContinuation upEveryone agrees.
    Perp-led rally, spot not buyingUp, perps buying, spot notFade (down)Leverage alone often unwinds.
    Spot-led selloffDown ≥ 12 bps, spot selling, perps notContinuation downReal coins are being sold.
    Broad selling (spot + perps)Down, both sellingContinuation downEveryone agrees.
    Perp-led selloff, spot not sellingDown, perps selling, spot notFade (up)Shorts or long liquidations without real sellers.
    Spot buying while perps sellFlat (±6 bps), spot buying, perps sellingUpQuiet accumulation.
    Spot selling while perps buyFlat, spot selling, perps buyingDownDistribution into leveraged buyers.
    One thing that confuses people

    The leadership chip in the top bar and Flow tab is coloured by the direction of the move: any rally is green. The flags in the "Spot vs perps" lower pane are coloured by what Flowdeck expects next. So a "Perp-led rally" shows a green chip but a red flag.

    Worked example
    Last 5 min: price +18 bps · perps aggression +0.15 · spot aggression +0.01 Funding 0.035% · Coinbase premium −$6 · OI +900 BTC in 1h

    Price is up, perps are buying hard, spot is not (0.01 < 0.02): "Perp-led rally, spot not buying". Funding is high, US buyers are not paying up and lots of new positions were opened. Flowdeck expects a fade. Do not chase longs; look for a failed breakout (Setup C) at the next resistance.

    Lesson 14

    Tape, Signals and Accuracy tabs

    In one lineTape = every big order as it happens. Signals = Flowdeck's alerts and their track record. Accuracy = proof that the data on screen is right.

    When the accuracy badge turns red

    1. Look at which part is red. "Trades x/y" below y means at least one minute matched neither Binance's candle nor a fresh download of that minute's trades (or that re-check is still running). "Book" well below 100% means the order book drifted.
    2. One red minute after a reconnect is normal. Flowdeck downloads that minute's trades again to double-check, and the book repairs itself on the next check (every 30 s).
    3. Red that stays usually means a bad internet connection or a blocked exchange. Check your connection; restart Flowdeck.
    4. While it is red, trust the heatmap and footprint numbers less. Prices are still fine; sizes and delta may be off.
    Part 5 · Footprint & profiles

    Inside the candles and the shape of the day

    The footprint shows who won every price inside each candle. Volume profile, VWAP and TPO show where the market agrees on value. Together they give you the levels where trades happen.

    Lesson 15

    Footprint: X-ray of each candle

    In one lineEach candle is split into price rows; each row shows BTC sold at market (left) and bought at market (right). Imbalances, the bar POC and the statistics row tell you who controlled the bar.

    Practice tool

    Tap a cell

    One 1-minute bar, $10 rows
    Where the numbers come from
    • Flowdeck records every Binance trade into $1 price steps for each 1-minute bar, then groups them into your bar size and row size. At start-up it downloads the last 60,000 trades (about 10–40 minutes); after that it records live. Per-price detail is kept 24 hours; older bars show as plain candles.
    • Bars: 1, 3, 5, 15, 30 minutes, 1 hour, 4 hours. Rows: Auto (the smallest of $1, 2, 5, 10, 25, 50, 100, 250, 500 that keeps rows at least 15 px tall) or a fixed size.
    • Source: Binance · All perps (Binance, COIN-M, Bybit, OKX, each shifted by its basis) · Spot (Binance spot + Coinbase). Other exchanges are recorded only while Flowdeck runs (kept 6 hours). Trade counts exist for Binance only.

    What each "Show" mode displays

    Imbalances: why the comparison is diagonal

    A market buy takes the ask; a market sell hits the bid. At any moment the ask is one step above the bid. So to compare buyers and sellers who were fighting at the same moment, Flowdeck compares the buys in one row with the sells one row lower.

    That is why the imbalance edge sits on the right of a cell for buyers and on the left for sellers.

    Imbalance rule
    • Buy imbalance at row r: buys(r) ≥ ratio × sells(r − 1 row).
    • Sell imbalance at row r: sells(r) ≥ ratio × buys(r + 1 row).
    • Ratio default 300% (Layers ▾ → Imb.: 150–500%). The cell must be more than 4% of the bar's biggest cell, so tiny cells don't count. A zero on the other side counts, as long as that neighbouring row traded at all (so a bar's bottom row can never be a buy imbalance, nor its top row a sell imbalance).
    • Stacked imbalance: 3 or more in a row on the same side. Becomes a zone that stretches right until a later bar trades back into it.
    The other marks
    • Bar POC (amber box): the row with the most volume in that bar.
    • Unfinished auction (blue dashed "unfinished"): both buyers and sellers traded in the bar's top row (or bottom row). A "finished" extreme has zero on one side: one side gave up there. The line stays until a later bar trades beyond it.
    • nPOC (amber line): a bar POC that no later bar has touched yet.
    • Absorption: violet box with "absorb X". Liquidations: small diamonds on the cell's left edge (orange = mostly long liquidations).
    • Filter (Off, 0.5–10 BTC): dims cells below the size so big ones stand out. Cluster (Off, 5–250 BTC): amber glow around every cell at least that big: big players' fingerprints.
    • Zones, unfinished lines and nPOCs are worked out only from the bars on your screen.

    The statistics row

    RowExactlyHow to use it
    TimeBar start time; the live bar shows a countdown.–
    VolumeAll BTC traded in the bar.Compare with the bars before: a spike shows interest.
    DeltaMarket buys minus market sells.Green = buyers pushed harder.
    Δ changeThis bar's delta minus the previous bar's.Momentum of aggression.
    Max Δ / Min ΔHighest and lowest running delta inside the bar (exact for Binance at any bar size; per minute for other sources).Max Δ +120 that ends at −10 = buyers tried hard and were absorbed.
    TradesNumber of Binance aggregate trades (fills of one order at one price count once).Many small trades = retail; few trades with big volume = size.
    Buy %Buy volume ÷ total volume.Above 60% or below 40% is one-sided.
    Stacked imb.Number of stacked imbalances: "2B" = two buy stacks, "1S" = one sell stack.Initiative by one side.
    OI ΔOpen-interest change of all exchanges during the bar, labelled new longs / new shorts / longs out / shorts out.Lesson 12.
    Liquidations"L x S y": BTC of long and short liquidations in the bar.Forced flow.
    CVDRunning delta from the first bar on your screen.Divergences across bars.

    Read a footprint bar in six steps

    1. Delta and Buy %: who was more aggressive, and by how much compared with volume?
    2. Where is the POC? At the top of a green bar: buyers met heavy selling at the high. At the bottom of a red bar: sellers met heavy buying at the low.
    3. Imbalances and stacks: stacked buy imbalances = buyers lifting several prices in a row (initiative).
    4. The extremes: finished (zero on one side) or unfinished (both sides traded)?
    5. Max Δ / Min Δ vs final delta: did one side push and then fail?
    6. OI Δ and liquidations: were new positions opened, or was it closing and forced flow?
    Worked example (the practice bar above)
    Volume 127.4 · Delta +41.8 (buy 66%) · POC 85,040 · stacked buy imbalance 85,040–85,060 Top row 85,080: 1.8 × 2.1 (unfinished) · bottom row 85,000: 0.0 × 1.4 (finished low)

    Buyers controlled this bar: strong positive delta, three stacked buy imbalances, and no sellers left at the low. The top is unfinished, so price is likely to trade above 85,080 again. The green zone 85,040–85,060 becomes support: if price comes back there and holds, it is a long location.

    Beginner mistakes
    • Reading single cells. Read the bar as a whole, then the bars around it.
    • Using 1-minute bars on a busy day with $1 rows. Too much detail; use Auto rows or 5-minute bars to see structure.
    • Expecting every imbalance zone to hold. Zones in the direction of the bigger trend hold more often.
    Lesson 16

    Six footprint patterns

    In one lineA handful of footprint shapes repeat every day. Learn to spot them and you know who is winning before the candle closes.

    Each pattern is drawn as one example bar ($10 rows; left = sold at market, right = bought at market). The violet outline marks the cells that matter.

    Lesson 17

    Volume profile: where the market agrees

    In one lineThe profile shows how much traded at each price. The POC is the "fair" price, the value area holds 70% of the volume, and old levels from previous days act as support, resistance and magnets.

    The volume profile turns the chart sideways: a bar for every price, as long as the BTC traded there. It sits on the left of the heatmap and on the right of the footprint.

    • POC (point of control): the price with the most volume. The "fair price". Price is often drawn back to it.
    • Value area (VAH to VAL): where 70% of volume traded. Inside = fair, outside = expensive or cheap.
    • High-volume nodes (thick parts): price slows down and chops. Low-volume nodes (thin parts): price moves through quickly.
    How the value area is built (Flowdeck's exact method)
    • Start at the POC row.
    • Look at the next two rows above and the next two rows below. Add whichever pair has more volume.
    • Repeat until the value area holds 70% of all volume. VAH = top of the highest row added; VAL = bottom of the lowest.
    • Session = the UTC day, starting at 05:30 IST. Bars without tick detail spread their candle volume evenly from low to high.
    Practice tool

    Build a value area yourself

    Press "Next step"

    Profile shapes

    Levels from earlier days

    Prior levels rules
    • Built from Binance volume with $10 rows, per UTC day.
    • pVAH / pVAL (dashed blue) and pPOC (amber) are yesterday's. "pPOC naked" in yellow = price has not touched it since.
    • Older days (up to 1, 3, 5 or 7 days, default 3) are drawn only if their POC is still naked: "nPOC 01 Oct 84,210". Naked = no later bar's range included it.
    • A "~" in front (for example "~pVAH") means that day had no tick detail, so its profile was built from 1-minute candles. Close, not exact.
    • Developing POC (Layers ▾, off by default): today's POC minute by minute, as an amber dotted step line. A rising developing POC = value moving up.

    Profile range

    Session (today, UTC) · Prior day · 4h · 1h · Visible · 3-day · 7-day. Layers ▾ → Volume profile.

    Profile type

    Volume · Delta (who won each price: green buyers, red sellers) · Liquidations (where people got wiped) · Spot vs perps (each side scaled on its own).

    Range profile tool

    Toolbar → Range profile, drag across at least 60 seconds. You get a box with its own POC, VAH/VAL and the label "Range · vol X · Δ ±Y · POC Z". Up to 6; right-click to delete.

    How traders use the profile

    1. Where did today open? Above yesterday's value area = buyers in control; inside = expect a range between pVAH and pVAL; below = sellers in control.
    2. Edges are for fading, the middle is for waiting. On range days, VAH and VAL are where reversals start; the POC is where they end.
    3. Acceptance or rejection? Price that leaves value and stays out for an hour or more is accepted: value is moving. Price that pokes out and comes straight back is rejected.
    4. The "80% rule" traders talk about: when price opens outside yesterday's value, comes back inside and holds for two 30-minute periods, it often travels to the other side of the value area. Often, not always.
    5. Naked POCs are targets, not entries.
    Beginner mistakes
    • Trading in the middle of the value area. Nothing is cheap or expensive there.
    • Forgetting the session starts at 05:30 IST. Early in the day the session profile is tiny and the prior-day levels matter more.
    • Using the 7-day profile for a 5-minute trade. Match the profile range to how long you plan to hold.
    Lesson 18

    VWAP: the average price big funds watch

    In one lineVWAP is the average price everyone paid today, weighted by size. Above it buyers are winning the day, below it sellers are; the σ bands show how stretched price is.

    Exactly how Flowdeck calculates it
    • VWAP = Σ(price × volume) ÷ Σ(volume) from the anchor: Daily = 00:00 UTC (05:30 IST), Weekly = Monday 00:00 UTC. Binance volume.
    • Where tick detail exists, every $1 price step counts with its own volume; older minutes use (high + low + close) ÷ 3.
    • σ = √( Σ(price² × volume) ÷ Σ(volume) − VWAP² ): the volume-weighted standard deviation. Bands at ±1σ, ±2σ, ±3σ.
    Worked example: three trades
    2 BTC at 85,000 · 1 BTC at 85,300 · 1 BTC at 84,900 VWAP = (2×85,000 + 85,300 + 84,900) ÷ 4 = 340,200 ÷ 4 = 85,050 Plain average of the three prices = 85,066.7 (VWAP leans to the 2 BTC trade) σ = √( (2×50² + 250² + 150²) ÷ 4 ) = √22,500 = 150 Bands = +1σ 85,200 · +2σ 85,350 · −1σ 84,900 · −2σ 84,750

    Trend day

    Price stays on one side of VWAP for hours. Pullbacks to VWAP (or to ±1σ) are where the trend resumes. The bands keep widening.

    Range day

    Price crosses VWAP again and again. ±2σ is stretched; price often snaps back toward VWAP. Fading the bands works here (Setup F).

    Anchored VWAP

    An anchored VWAP (violet "aVWAP", no bands) starts from a moment you choose and shows the average price of everyone who traded since then. If price is above it, those buyers are in profit and tend to defend it.

    Anchor… presetStarts atUse it for
    Weekly openMonday 00:00 UTC (05:30 IST)Who is winning the week.
    Daily open00:00 UTC (05:30 IST)Same start as the daily VWAP; useful when the daily VWAP is off.
    Last fundingThe latest 00/08/16 UTC funding timeThe average price of the current 8-hour window.
    Last big liquidation30 s before the latest cascade (or the biggest single liquidation if there was none)Where the panic buyers or sellers got in. A favourite level after flushes.
    Anchor VWAP toolAny point you click (snapped to the minute; up to 4)A swing high or low, a news spike, the start of a trend.
    Beginner mistakes
    • Shorting just because price is above +2σ on a trend day. On trend days price can ride the bands.
    • Expecting the daily VWAP to matter early in the UTC day. After 30 minutes it is built from very little volume.
    • Anchoring at random points. Anchor at moments that mattered: a big low, a cascade, a breakout.
    Lesson 19

    TPO: where price spent its time

    In one lineEach letter is 30 minutes. Many letters in a row = price spent a long time there (accepted). Single letters = price moved fast (rejected or unfinished).

    Practice tool

    Which half hour is each letter?

    A and B = initial balance
    Exact rules
    • Periods are 30 minutes. Letters A–X cover the first 12 hours of the session, then a–x. Built from Binance 1-minute highs and lows.
    • Initial balance (IB) = the range of the first two periods (the first hour). Amber rail; IB letters in yellow; the current period in white.
    • Single prints = rows touched by only one period, not counting the tails at the very top and bottom. Violet.
    • Excess = two or more single-letter rows at the high or low. Needs at least two periods, and a tail made only of the current period does not count.
    • Poor high / low = the extreme row was touched by two or more periods (only when there is no excess).
    • POC = row with the most letters; value area = 70% of letters, built the same way as in Lesson 17.
    • Footer: range, IB size, POC, value area, single prints, and "range ext. up / down" (closed beyond the IB) or "inside IB".
    Session presetUTCIndia time (IST)
    UTC day00:00–24:0005:30–05:30 next day
    Asia00:00–08:0005:30–13:30
    London07:00–16:0012:30–21:30
    New York13:30–20:0019:00–01:30 (the US stock market opens 1 hour later in winter: 20:00 IST)
    Funding 8h00–08, 08–16, 16–2405:30–13:30, 13:30–21:30, 21:30–05:30

    Four kinds of day

    Normal day

    The first hour (IB) sets most of the range; later letters stay inside or extend a little. Trade: fade the IB high and low.

    Trend day

    Small IB, then price keeps extending one way; the profile is long and thin with few letters per row. Trade: follow it, buy pullbacks, never fade.

    Double distribution

    Two fat areas with single prints between them: value moved during the day. Trade: the single prints are support or resistance on a retest.

    Neutral day

    Price extends above and below the IB, then closes in the middle. Trade: both sides got trapped; expect a range tomorrow.

    Beginner mistakes
    • Reading letters as times in your local clock. Letters follow the session start in UTC; use the converter above.
    • Calling excess on the live session too early. The current period can still add letters.
    • Ignoring poor highs and lows. They are unfinished business; price often returns to break them.
    Part 6 · Options

    How options dealers move price

    One lesson, but an important one: on many days the gamma levels decide whether BTC ranges or trends.

    Lesson 20

    Gamma: how options dealers move price

    In one lineDealers who sold options must keep buying and selling BTC as price moves. In positive gamma their hedging calms price down; in negative gamma it speeds price up.

    An option is a contract that pays if BTC ends above a price (a call) or below a price (a put). That price is the strike. Big banks and market makers sell most of them on Deribit. They do not want to bet on direction, so they hedge: they hold some BTC (or perps) against each option.

    The amount they need changes as price moves. Gamma measures how fast it changes. Near big strikes and near expiry, gamma is large, so dealers must trade a lot of BTC for a small move.

    Think of a thermostat. In positive gamma, dealers act like a thermostat: price up → they sell, price down → they buy, so the room stays at the same temperature. In negative gamma the thermostat is wired backwards: price down → they sell, price up → they buy, and the temperature runs away.
    How Flowdeck calculates it
    • Every 60 seconds it downloads all BTC options from Deribit: open interest, implied volatility (mark IV) and the underlying price.
    • For each option it computes Black-Scholes gamma, then GEX = gamma × OI (BTC) × price² × 1%: the dollars of BTC dealers would have to buy or sell for a 1% move.
    • Calls count positive, puts negative. This assumes dealers are long calls and short puts (they bought calls from and sold puts to their clients). It is the usual assumption, but real positions are not public, so it can be wrong.
    • Net GEX = the sum over all strikes. Positive = positive gamma regime.
    • Gamma flip: Flowdeck recalculates total GEX at imaginary prices from −20% to +20% in 0.25% steps and finds where it crosses zero, nearest to the current price.
    • Call wall = strike with the largest call GEX; put wall = strike with the most negative put GEX; both within ±35% of price. ±γ lines = the 3 biggest positive and negative strikes.
    • Max pain = for the nearest expiry only, the price where option buyers would collect the least.
    • Expiries: All expiries · Next expiry · ≤ 7 days · ≤ 35 days. Deribit options expire at 08:00 UTC = 13:30 IST.
    • Deribit uses its own index price. "Shift to perp price" (on by default) moves the lines on the chart by the basis so they sit at the right Binance price; the Gamma tab shows the raw Deribit numbers.
    Line on the chartLooks likeHow it usually behaves
    Call wallGreen dashedA ceiling in positive gamma: dealers sell more as price rises into it. If price breaks it with force, the ceiling can turn into a launch pad.
    Put wallRed dashedA floor in positive gamma. A break below often accelerates, because hedging flips to selling.
    Gamma flipAmberAbove it: calm, mean-reverting. Below it: faster, trending moves.
    Max painGrey dottedPrice sometimes drifts toward it into the nearest expiry, mostly on quiet days.
    +γ / −γThin linesBig strikes where price tends to stick (+) or slip (−).
    Worked example
    Net GEX +$38M per 1% · price 85,000 If BTC drops 1% (−$850), dealers buy about $38M ≈ 447 BTC to stay hedged. If BTC rises 1%, they sell about the same amount.

    That is a cushion of ~450 BTC each way per 1%: a range day is likely. If net GEX were −$38M, the same 1% drop would make dealers sell ~447 BTC more, and the drop would feed itself.

    Using gamma, step by step

    1. At the start of your session, open the Gamma tab: positive or negative? Note the call wall, put wall and flip.
    2. Positive and price between the walls: expect a range. Fade moves into the walls and the VWAP bands (Setups A and F). Smaller targets.
    3. Negative, or price below the flip: expect trends and bigger ranges. Trade breakouts in the move's direction (Setup B), widen stops, cut size, avoid fading.
    4. Near expiry (especially the last Friday of the month, at 13:30 IST), big strikes pin price beforehand; after expiry that gamma disappears and moves can free up.
    5. Check every hour. Levels move as traders open and close options.
    Beginner mistakes
    • Treating the call wall as a guaranteed top. It is where hedging pressure is strongest, not a wall of orders.
    • Forgetting that only Deribit is included. CME and over-the-counter options are not in the numbers.
    • Reading the Gamma tab numbers against the Binance price. The tab is in Deribit index prices; the chart lines are shifted.
    Part 7 · Trading with it

    From reading the screen to taking a trade

    Where big players show themselves, a daily routine, what happens in common situations, six setups with exact steps, a full worked trade, risk control and a final test.

    Lesson 21

    Where are the big players?

    In one lineBig players cannot hide completely: their orders are too large. They split, hide and bluff, and each trick leaves a mark Flowdeck can show.

    ClueWhere to lookWhat it tells you
    WallsYellow, orange and red stripes, "W 104" tags, amber boxes in the ladder, Book tabWhere a big player wants to buy or sell. Real if it stays as price arrives; fake if pulled.
    Big market ordersNumbered circles, Tape highlights, CVD by size (≥ 10 BTC line)Urgent big money. Whale CVD rising while price dips = accumulation.
    IcebergsCyan ◇ on heatmap, Book tab eventsA hidden big order defending a price.
    AbsorptionViolet ▲ on heatmap, violet box and cluster cells in the footprintA passive giant soaking up the other side.
    Fresh positionsOI pane, OI Δ row, OI all venuesOI up with price up = new longs; OI up with price down = new shorts.
    Real spot moneySpot vs perps CVD, Coinbase premium, Flow leadershipFunds buying actual Bitcoin, not leverage.
    Options dealersGamma tab, call/put walls, flipForced hedging that pins price or speeds it up.
    Stop and liquidation poolsLiquidation model, poor highs/lows, yesterday's high and lowWhere forced orders sit. Big players often push price there to fill their own orders.

    Their five tricks, and how to catch each one

    1 · Splitting the order

    What they do
    Buy 500 BTC as hundreds of 1–5 BTC orders over an hour, so no single print looks big.
    Flowdeck tell
    "CVD by order size": the 1–10 BTC line climbs steadily while price barely moves. Delta by size in the Flow tab leans one way for 1 hour.

    2 · Hiding it (iceberg)

    What they do
    Show 3 BTC, refill again and again.
    Flowdeck tell
    Cyan ◇ "iceberg X (Y hidden)"; the Book tab's hidden total grows; price keeps bouncing off one exact price.

    3 · Bluffing (spoof)

    What they do
    Place a huge bid to make sellers nervous and buyers confident, then cancel it before it trades, often while selling.
    Flowdeck tell
    Amber ✕ "pulled N" within 8 bps of price; walls that keep the same distance from price; red pull/stack at the wall.

    4 · Hunting stops

    What they do
    Push price through an obvious high or low where stops and liquidations sit, buy from the forced sellers (or sell to the forced buyers), then let price return.
    Flowdeck tell
    A liquidation cluster or poor low just beyond the level; a burst of orange diamonds; absorption at the new low; price closes back inside. That is Setup C or D.

    5 · Buying real coins quietly

    What they do
    Funds buy spot on Coinbase and Binance spot while perps traders are bearish.
    Flowdeck tell
    Coinbase premium positive and rising, spot CVD up while perps CVD is flat or down, "Spot buying while perps sell". That is Setup E.
    Lesson 22

    A daily routine (India time)

    In one lineTen minutes of preparation decide most of your results: know the context and mark the levels before price gets there.

    • 05:3000:00 UTC
      New UTC day. Session profile, daily VWAP and TPO restart. Funding is paid. Yesterday's VAH/POC/VAL become pVAH/pPOC/pVAL.
    • 05:30–12:30Asia
      Usually the quietest stretch. Ranges, thin books, more spoofs. Smaller size.
    • 12:3007:00 UTC
      London opens. Volume picks up; the Asian range often breaks.
    • 13:3008:00 UTC
      Funding and Deribit option expiry (daily; big ones on Fridays, biggest on the last Friday of the month).
    • 18:00 / 19:00US data
      Big US data such as inflation (CPI) comes out at 18:00 IST in US summer time, 19:00 in winter. Books thin out before; the first minute is chaos. Stay flat.
    • 19:00 / 20:00US open
      US stock market opens (summer / winter). Usually the busiest hours; ETF and fund flows show in the Coinbase premium.
    • 21:3016:00 UTC
      Funding. London closes. Moves often pause.
    • 23:30 / 00:30FOMC days
      US Federal Reserve decisions (8 times a year). Same rule as data: no trades into the release.
    • Weekend
      Lower volume, thinner books, CME futures closed. Walls are easier to spoof; moves can be sudden. Half size or stay out.

    Before you trade: the 10-minute preparation

    1. Data check: Live, green accuracy dot, Book near 100%.
    2. Gamma tab: regime (positive or negative), flip, call wall, put wall. Write them down.
    3. Flow tab: OI-weighted funding, Coinbase premium, OI change in the last hour, spot vs perps delta for 1 hour, the leadership card.
    4. Levels: where is price compared with yesterday's value area (pVAH, pPOC, pVAL)? Any naked POCs within 1–2%? Where are VWAP and its bands?
    5. Liquidation map: the biggest long cluster below and short cluster above.
    6. Write the plan in one line per idea: "If price reaches level and I see trigger, I will long/short with stop at X and target Y." Then wait. No plan, no trade.
    Example plan
    Context: positive gamma (+$42M), funding 0.010%, CB premium +$12 → range day Levels: pVAH 85,420 · pPOC 85,080 · pVAL 84,520 · put wall 84,000 · call wall 86,000 Long idea: at pVAL 84,520 if a bid wall holds or absorption appears → stop 84,470, targets 85,080 / 85,350 Short idea: at pVAH 85,420 if the ask holds and CVD diverges → stop 85,480, target 85,080 Not today: breakouts (positive gamma), anything in the middle (84,700–85,250)

    After the session

    Spend five minutes on the journal (Lesson 26): screenshot each trade, write the setup letter, what the screen showed, and whether you followed the plan. Do not judge a trade by its result; judge it by whether you followed the plan.

    Lesson 23

    What happens if…

    In one lineMost situations have only two or three ways to play out. Know them in advance and you react instead of guessing.

    Pick a situation. Each lists where to look, the possible outcomes, what each one means, what to do, and what confirms it.

    Lesson 24

    The trade playbook

    In one lineSix setups. Each needs the right context, a real level, an order-flow trigger and a stop you decided before you clicked.

    Every good trade answers four questions in this order:

    1. Context: what kind of day is it? (gamma regime, spot vs perps, funding, trend or range)
    2. Location: am I at an important price? (POC, VAH/VAL, yesterday's levels, VWAP bands, gamma walls, liquidation clusters)
    3. Trigger: is order flow confirming? (walls holding or pulled, absorption, sweeps, imbalances, CVD)
    4. Risk: where am I wrong, and how much do I lose if I am?

    Missing one of the four? Skip the trade. Each setup below has a long and a short version, a worked example with numbers, and how to manage the trade.

    SetupDay typeTypical win rate neededTypical target
    A · Defended levelRange / positive gamma~40% at 1.5R+VWAP, POC
    B · Breakout + retestTrend / negative gamma~35% at 2R+Next nPOC, wall, cluster
    C · Failed break (trap)Any, best in range~40% at 1.5R+POC, other side of value
    D · Flush reversalAfter a cascade~35% at 2R+VWAP, cascade start
    E · Spot-led pullbackSpot-led trend~40% at 1.5R+Previous high, +2σ
    F · Fade the stretchRange / positive gamma~45% at 1.2R+VWAP

    "Win rate needed" is simply the break-even math for that reward-to-risk (Lesson 26), not a promise of results.

    Lesson 25

    One trade from start to finish

    In one lineA complete Setup A long, step by step: preparation, waiting, the trigger, sizing, managing and the journal. Then the same trade when it fails.

    The numbers are an illustration built to show the process clearly; they are not a real past trade. Use the dots or the buttons to move through the steps.

    Lesson 26

    Before you click buy or sell

    In one lineYour stop and your position size, not your entry, decide whether you survive long enough to get good.

    The honest truth

    No setup wins every time. Professional traders lose many trades; they make money because their losses are small and their wins are bigger. Practise on paper or with the smallest size first. This page is education, not financial advice.

    Why risk only 1%?

    Losing streaks happen to everyone. Account left after a streak:

    Risk per trade5 losses10 losses15 losses
    1%−4.9%−9.6%−14.0%
    2%−9.6%−18.3%−26.1%
    5%−22.6%−40.1%−53.7%
    10%−41.0%−65.1%−79.4%

    After −65% you need +186% just to get back to where you started.

    How often must you win?

    Break-even win rate for each reward-to-risk (before fees):

    Reward : riskWin rate to break even
    1R50%
    1.5R40%
    2R33%
    3R25%

    Formula: 1 ÷ (1 + R). Bigger targets let you be wrong more often, but they are hit less often too.

    Position size, the right way round
    • 1. Decide where you are wrong (the stop), from the chart. 2. Decide how much money you accept losing (1% of the account). 3. Size = money at risk ÷ (stop distance + fees per BTC).
    • Leverage is only the result: position value ÷ account. Make sure the exchange's liquidation price is far beyond your stop.
    • Fees count. With market orders both ways (0.05% + 0.05%) you pay about $85 per BTC at 85,000. On a $100 stop that almost doubles the loss per BTC. A limit entry (maker) saves about $25 per BTC.
    Trade quality0 / 12
    Tick what is true for your trade idea.

    Position size calculator

    Managing a trade once you are in

    1. Do nothing for the first minute unless the stop is hit. Noise is not information.
    2. At +1R (or at the first level such as VWAP), move the stop to break-even plus fees. Now the trade cannot lose.
    3. At target 1, take half off. Let the rest run to target 2 or until the order flow turns (wall holds against you, absorption on the other side, CVD divergence).
    4. Never widen the stop. If the reason for the trade is gone (wall pulled, level lost), exit early even before the stop.

    Golden rules

    • Risk 0.5–1% of your account per trade.
    • Decide the stop before you enter. Never move it further away.
    • Take trades with at least 1.5× more reward than risk, after fees.
    • Stop for the day after 2 losses in a row, or −2% on the day.

    Avoid

    • Trading in the middle of the value area with no level nearby.
    • Catching a liquidation cascade while it is still running.
    • High leverage "because the setup is perfect".
    • Trading the first minutes after big news.
    • Trading on Demo data.

    Journal template

    • Date, time (IST), setup letter, long/short
    • Context: gamma, funding, premium, leadership
    • Level and trigger (screenshot)
    • Entry, stop, targets, size, R planned
    • Result in R; followed the plan? yes/no
    • One lesson
    Lesson 27

    Questions people ask

    The top bar says "Demo feed". Why?

    The server is running in demo mode, so every price and trade is simulated. On flowdeck.site you should always see Live; if you see Demo feed there, contact us.

    The accuracy dot is red.

    At least one recent minute matched neither Binance's candle nor a fresh download of its trades, or the book check found differences. After a reconnect this is normal and clears. If it stays red, check your internet and restart Flowdeck (Lesson 14).

    The feeds keep saying "reconnecting".

    Binance futures may be blocked on your network or in your country. Check that binance.com futures open in your browser.

    I see no numbered circles.

    Big trade is set higher than today's orders (Layers ▾ → Big trade); try 5 BTC. Circles from other exchanges also need "Other venues' prints" on and that exchange ticked in the Tape tab.

    My heatmap looks different from older screenshots (teal and white, pie bubbles).

    That is the older look. Layers ▾ → Heatmap → Colours Classic gives the blue → red price rows, and Layers ▾ → Bubbles → 3D with Grouping Smart gives the round balls. Pick Thermal, Buy/sell pie and Grouping Off to go back.

    Bubbles cover the heatmap.

    Move the green bubble-size slider on the toolbar to the left, or raise Layers ▾ → Bubbles → Transparency. Volume delta sizing also makes balls smaller when buyers and sellers were equal.

    I see no walls, W tags or ✕ markers.

    Layers ▾ → Walls & icebergs is off. The coloured stripes on the heatmap still show; the markers need this switch.

    The heatmap is empty on the left.

    Heatmap history starts when the server starts and keeps 30 minutes. Leave Flowdeck running (the server keeps recording with the tab closed).

    Old footprint bars are plain candles.

    Per-price detail exists for about 10–40 minutes before start-up and everything after it, kept for 24 hours. Older bars only have candles.

    My CVD number changed after I reloaded.

    The lower-pane CVD starts from what your browser loaded (up to 30 minutes back), and the footprint CVD from the first bar on screen. Read the direction and shape, not the number.

    The gamma lines are missing.

    Layers ▾ → Gamma levels is off, or Deribit has not answered yet (it refreshes every 60 seconds).

    Why are Binance liquidation totals so small?

    Binance publishes at most one liquidation per second per contract. Bybit and OKX publish all of them. Look at the all-venue totals.

    Why is Flowdeck's price different from my TradingView chart?

    Flowdeck uses Binance's BTCUSDT perpetual (last trade). Your chart may show spot, another exchange, the mark price or the index. A few dollars of difference is normal.

    What time zone are the times in?

    Chart times are your computer's local time. Sessions, VWAP and profiles are fixed in UTC: the day starts at 05:30 IST.

    Can Flowdeck tell me where price will go?

    No. It shows what is happening in the order book and the trades, very accurately. That gives you better odds at good locations, not certainty. Every signal it scores (absorption, leadership) shows its real hit rate so you can judge it yourself.

    What settings should a beginner use?

    The defaults, with Big trade at 5 BTC (10 on busy days), Min at 0.2–0.5 BTC, Lower pane "Delta + CVD", and the Tape tab open. Add one layer at a time.

    Is there a "best" timeframe for the footprint?

    1-minute bars for timing an entry at a level, 5-minute bars to see the structure of the last hour, 15–30 minutes to see the day. Rows on Auto.

    Lesson 28

    Test yourself

    Twenty questions across the whole manual. The explanation appears after you answer. Score 16 or more and you can read the dashboard.

    Glossary

    Screenshots come from Flowdeck's demo mode (a simulated market), so prices and sizes are made up. Your live screen shows the same panels with real data. The exact rules on this page are taken from the Flowdeck code (October 2026 version).

    Flowdeck reads public data from Binance, Bybit, OKX, Coinbase and Deribit. Nothing on this page is financial advice.
